Talking About Reasons And Results
You can talk about reasons and results in both speaking and writing by using various expressions and structures.
I was just calling because I wanted to find out how the cleanse is going.
There are several expressions that you can use to talk about the cause of a situation or its effect.

Some of the most common words to introduce reasons are: because, since, and as.
You can also introduce the reason or cause of a situation with:
because of/ owing to/ due to
thanks to (this can be used both in positive situations or in a negative way)

• The baby woke up because of/ due to the loud noise from the party downstairs.
  • Owing to the loud noise from the party downstairs, the baby woke up.
  • Thanks to the loan from the bank, the company was able to rent an office space. (positive situation)
  • The house is a mess thanks to you and your friends. (not really thankful)

If you want to talk about the effect of a situation, you can use so, as a result, and therefore.
You can also use:
the cause of…is
….is caused by/ is due to…

•
  • The cause of obesity is inactivity and unhealthy eating habits.
  • Obesity is caused by/ is due to to inactivity and unhealthy eating habits.

Remember that some expressions are followed by a clause:
because
since
as
therefore

Other expressions are followed by a noun:
because of
due to
owing to
thanks to
That happens during a cleanse since your body is trying to get used to a change.
Due to the sudden lack of caffeine, your body is experiencing withdrawal.
Thanks to all the fresh fruit and raw vegetables I'm eating, I feel much more energetic.
She decided to do this cleanse due to your commitment.
Reporting Other People's Words and Thoughts

You can report other people's thoughts or words by using your own words or saying exactly what they said. There are several reporting verbs that can be used with a that-clause and objects, as well as different structures for reporting questions and negatives.
You indicated that you would have trouble forgoing caffeine.

You can say what someone else thinks or says by using their exact words. When you do this, you need to put their words in quotation marks. The quotation can come before or after the reporting clause with the reporting verb. You can also put the quotation on either side of the reporting clause.

• “I missed the bus and I was late for work today,” complained Anna.
  • Anna complained, “I missed the bus and was I late for work today.”
  • “I missed the bus, ” complained Anna, “and I was late for work today.”
You can use a that-clause after most reporting verbs.
The gymnast said that she had been doing gymnastics since she was 2 years old.
In speaking or informal usage, it is okay to leave out that. You can also leave out that with the common reporting verbs: agree, mention, promise, notice and warn.

The actor said (that) he was excited about working with Angelina Jolie.
The director mentioned (that) the movie was going to cost two million dollars to make.
You should not leave out that:
→ in formal writing

→ with verbs like: answer, argue, complain, reply, warn, deny, confide, speculate and grumble.
The teacher speculated that one of her students had stolen the exam from her bag.
The student she suspected denied that he had taken anything from her bag.
He argued that he had been playing basketball in the gym that afternoon.

→ when the that-clause does not come right after the verb
The woman told her son thatshe was not going to live in a home for senior citizens when she got older.
He promised his mother that she would be able to live with him.

Some verbs do not require an object before the that-clause.
  • The man remarked that reading a book was one of the best ways to relax.

It is not always necessary to put an object after the reporting verbs promise, teach, show, warn and advise.
  • I overheard my mother talking with my father. He promised (her) that he would be home early if the meeting got cancelled.

But for reporting verbs like, inform, notify, convince, tell, assure, remind, reassure and persuade, an object before the that-clause is necessary.
  • My parents informed the school that I would not be attending classes this morning.
    • He told his wife that he would be home late.
Some verbs also require a preposition after the verb if you want to include a personal object before the that-clause.

Sometimes you want to say what someone didn't say. You can make the reporting verb negative.
  • She didn't talk about her vacation. (nothing was said about her vacation) .

If what the person said was negative, you can either make the reported clause negative, or make the reporting verb negative.
  • “My vacation wasn't great,” thought Laura. She didn't think her vacation was great. OR She thought her vacation wasn't great.
If you want to report when someone asks a wh-word question, you can use the question word in the reported clause. If someone asks a yes/ no question, use if or whether in the reported clause.

• Where did you go on vacation?” asked John.
    John asked (me) where I went on vacation.     (do not use a form of ‘do in the reported clause)

• “Is this seat taken?” asked the old woman.
    The old woman asked if/ whether this seat was taken.

• “Who is the best actress in Hollywood?” asked my teacher.
    My teacher asked who the best actress in Hollywood was. OR My teacher asked who was the best actress in Hollywood.     (you can put the complement before or after the form of ‘be' in wh-questions with who, which or what)

Peter: Hello?
Vanessa: Hi Peter. I was just calling because I wanted to find out how the cleanse is going.
Peter: It's going pretty well. I've been really resolved to sticking to the diet and not having any sugar or dairy or meat. It's really difficult to eliminate those things but I'm doing my best.
Vanessa: You indicated that you would have trouble forgoing caffeine. How is that going?
Peter: Well, that's been a hard addiction to break. I've had a lot of headaches and a few friends have told me that I'm a bit moody. If I could still have java, I would be happier, but I understand that caffeine isn't healthy.

Vanessa: Yes, that happens during a cleanse since your body is trying to get used to a change. Due to the sudden lack of caffeine, your body is experiencing withdrawal. It will pass. If it were easy to break these addictions, we wouldn't have to do a cleanse!
Peter: Other than that, I feel pretty good. Thanks to all the fresh fruit and raw vegetables I'm eating, I feel much more energetic.
Vanessa: That's great! Once you have gotten rid of toxins in your body you will feel much better. My doctor persuaded me to eat raw vegetables at every meal and I really feel the difference. How about Amy? She decided to do this cleanse due to your commitment.

Peter: She confided that she has cheated a couple times. If she didn't have to go without wine, she would be happier! She has gone out with friends a couple times and had a glass of wine. She assured me that it was only one glass. She said she's eating lots of vegetables and drinking more water than she used to.
Vanessa: Well, I think you've both done really well. I'm very proud of you both!
